messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

María had lived in the United States for decades, but the fear that settled into her body belonged to the years before she arrived. She was a young mother in a refugee camp after fleeing political violence in Latin America, sleeping in crowded quarters where every sound mattered and where the air itself seemed to carry danger. One night, during a chaotic sweep through the camp, she was separated from her children for hours while soldiers shouted, doors banged, and people ran. What she remembered most vividly was not a clear story but fragments: the sharp, stale smell of sweat, dust, and fuel; the pressure in her chest; the sense that she could not make sense of what was happening or find words for it even later. Even now, when she tries to tell it, María says she cannot put the event into language without feeling as if she is back inside it. When the memory comes, it brings a wave of intense guilt, because she has long been certain she should have kept her children safer.

Over the years, those fragments have remained powerful because they still feel dangerously present. A smell in the hallway of her apartment building, the odor of diesel from a passing truck, or the faint chemical scent of cleaning products in the library can pull her back into the camp before she has time to steady herself. In those moments she becomes superalert, scanning corners, listening for raised voices, and watching the faces of strangers as if something might happen at any second. At the library where she worked for many years, María would sit rigidly at the circulation desk, struggling to follow conversations when her attention kept drifting to the entrance, the sound of footsteps, or the feel of someone standing too close behind her. She had come to believe that safety existed only in a very limited number of places, and even there she remained on guard.

That constant watchfulness has shaped the way she tries to cope. María keeps herself busy on purpose, filling her days with chores, prayer, sorting papers, and small tasks around the house so there is little room for the memories to catch her. When she sits still, she begins to go over the event again and again, asking why it happened to her, why she did not do more, why she lost sight of her children that night. The more she thinks this way, the more the old images and sensations return: the smell, the helplessness, the unspoken terror. She finds that the harder she pushes the experience away by staying occupied, the more it seems to push back through her body and dreams, until she is left with the same wordless, guilty recollection she has spent years trying to outrun.

That cycle has made ordinary life smaller. María avoids crowded places, certain streets near her apartment, and even some areas of the library where the aisles feel too enclosed and she cannot see who is coming. She no longer stays late for events, and she has begun refusing errands that would take her beyond the few places where she feels remotely safe. Her husband notices that she is tense at dinner, distracted when he speaks, and often absent-mindedly rubbing her hands together as if trying to keep herself in the room. She is most troubled by how hard it is to concentrate now; while reading to catalog books or paying bills, her mind drifts to the camp, then to questions about what she should have done differently. Those moments of self-blame feed her vigilance, and her vigilance keeps the memories alive.

María finally sought help after a recent afternoon at the library, when a strong cleaning smell in the stacks brought the scene back with such force that she had to hide in the restroom until her hands stopped shaking. Since then she has felt increasingly trapped between her need to stay busy, her inability to settle her mind, and the fear that the world outside the small circle of places she still trusts is waiting to overwhelm her again. What she most wants is relief from the guilt and the constant scanning, but what frightens her most is that if she lets herself remember fully, she will be swallowed by the same terror she survived long ago.
